question:
How should test inputs be chosen for a function that accepts numeric values within a valid range?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:
[JEV filter] kept 7 of 7 guidelines (JEV 'lenient' score > 0.5)

# Guidelines
- Partition the input domain into equivalence classes (valid and invalid) and select at least one representative test case from each class. For a numeric range, this means at minimum one value inside the valid range, one below it, and one above it. (source: root/Software Testing Methodologies and Techniques/Software Testing Approaches and Techniques/Classification and Specification-Based Testing Techniques.md; root/Software Testing Methodologies and Techniques/Boundary Value Analysis and Syntax Testing Techniques.md) [JEV 0.92]
- Choose test cases [SWEBOK excerpt bb061752587bc7b35163] (boundary value analysis), because [SWEBOK excerpt 44266d1663bca03e93fd]. (source: root/Software Testing Methodologies and Techniques/Boundary Value Analysis and Syntax Testing Techniques.md) [JEV 0.98]
- Extend boundary value testing with robustness testing by also choosing test cases outside the valid input domain, to verify the program handles unexpected or erroneous inputs correctly. (source: root/Software Testing Methodologies and Techniques/Boundary Value Analysis and Syntax Testing Techniques.md) [JEV 0.97]
- Include test cases specifically designed to force exceptions, such as overflow or underflow conditions, to verify that the function can manage predefined numeric error conditions and generate appropriate error messages. (source: root/Testing Methodologies and Quality Assurance Practices/Testing Approaches and Execution Strategies/Software Testing Techniques and Methodologies/Exception Testing and Error Handling in Software Testing.md) [JEV 0.96]
- Use combinatorial test techniques (e.g., pair-wise testing or all-combinations testing) to systematically derive test cases that cover specific parameter values or conditions when multiple numeric inputs interact. (source: root/Software Testing Methodologies and Techniques/Combinatorial Test Techniques Overview.md; root/Software Testing Methodologies and Techniques/Systematic Test Case Derivation and Combinatorial Methods/Combinatorial Testing and Decision Tables.md) [JEV 0.91]
- Supplement deterministic (specification-driven) test selection with randomly drawn inputs from the input domain. Random testing provides a simple approach to automation and can expose faults that structured techniques miss; enhanced forms such as adaptive random testing can further direct sampling. (source: root/Testing Methodologies and Quality Assurance Practices/Software Testing Techniques, Measurement, and Management/Testing Approaches and Test Case Selection Methods/Deterministic vs. Random Test Case Selection.md; root/Testing Methodologies and Quality Assurance Practices/Testing Approaches and Execution Strategies/Software Testing Techniques and Methodologies/Random Testing and Evidence-Based Software Engineering Approaches.md) [JEV 0.87]
- Combine specification-based (black-box) and structure-based (white-box) test case selection approaches, [SWEBOK excerpt 850132b272f72b31e5df], complementing each other. (source: root/Testing Methodologies and Quality Assurance Practices/Software Testing Techniques, Measurement, and Management/Testing Approaches and Test Case Selection Methods/Combining Functional and Structural Testing Techniques.md) [JEV 0.96]
